claims.text: Reduction kinetics govern the reliable formation of uniformly mixed, single-phase noble-metal high-entropy-alloy nanomaterials.
A uniformly mixed, single-phase alloy produces a consistent distribution of catalytically active sites.
A consistent distribution of active sites enhances catalytic performance.
Slow reduction allows more even nucleation than rapid reduction.
Slow reduction provides sufficient atomic interdiffusion to improve alloy mixing.
More even nucleation and atomic interdiffusion minimize local composition fluctuations.
Enhanced atomic mixing makes catalytically active sites more uniformly distributed.
Uniformly distributed active sites improve electron transfer during catalysis.
Uniformly distributed active sites improve mass transfer during catalysis.
Slowly reduced nanomaterials will exhibit more uniform alloy structures and less phase segregation than rapidly reduced materials.
Slowly reduced nanomaterials will have higher turnover frequencies or conversion rates than rapidly reduced materials.
Rapid reduction tends to produce heterogeneous phases with a non-uniform distribution of noble-metal sites.
The heterogeneous phases and non-uniform noble-metal-site distribution associated with rapid reduction lead to lower catalytic efficiency.
The proposed effect should hold for catalytic reactions that are strongly sensitive to surface composition and structural uniformity, including oxidation reactions.
Prior evidence supports the direction of improved homogeneity and catalytic performance under slow reduction.
